html:
After Britain took Lower Burma in 1852, settlers cleared the swamps and forests of the Irrawaddy delta for rice. By the early 20th century Burma was the world's largest exporter of rice.

The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 and steamships carried the rice to Europe and India. Millions of migrants from Upper Burma moved south, and Indian labourers and Chettiar moneylenders came too.

When the Depression of the 1930s crashed prices, many farmers lost their land to the moneylenders. Anger at this fed the Saya San rebellion and anti-Indian riots. Rice remains the staple and a key export. See British conquest and Irrawaddy River.
